quote: Python is typically implemented using a combination of a bytecode compiler and interpreter. Compilation is implicitly performed as modules are loaded, and several language primitives require the compiler to be available at run-time.
what: Python is typically implemented as a bytecode compiler plus interpreter, with compilation done implicitly as modules load, and several language primitives requiring the compiler to be present at run-time.

quote: In Python, variables are simply names that refer to objects.   Variables do not need to be declared before they are assigned and they can even change type in the middle of a program.
what: Python uses dynamic typing: variables are just names referring to objects, need no declaration, can change type mid-program, and all type checking happens at run-time by an interpreter rather than at a separate compile step.

quote: In Python, all objects that can be named are said to be "first class."
what: All objects that can be named in Python are "first class", so functions, classes, methods, modules and other named objects can be passed around, inspected, and placed in data structures at run-time.

quote: seemingly complicated tasks can often be expressed with very little code
what: A major appeal of Python and other dynamic languages is that seemingly complicated tasks can often be expressed with very little code.

quote: Python has an extensive standard library, which is one of the main reasons for its popularity.
what: An extensive, always-evolving standard library of more than 100 modules is named as one of the main reasons for Python's popularity.

quote: a high-level for statement that loops over any "iterable" object
what: The for statement is high-level, looping over any "iterable" object rather than over a numeric index.

quote: Python also has full support for object-oriented programming including user-defined classes, inheritance, and run-time binding of methods.
what: Python provides full object-oriented programming support, including user-defined classes, inheritance, and run-time binding of methods.

quote: These are all immutable types, meaning that values are represented by objects that cannot be modified after their creation.
what: Python's primitive built-in types (Booleans, numbers, strings) are immutable: their values are objects that cannot be modified after creation.

quote: instead of using braces for statement grouping, it uses indentation
what: Python departs from C-like languages by using indentation for statement grouping instead of braces, dispensing with braces and trailing semicolons.

quote: several other implementations have become popular. Jython is a version that runs on the JVM and has seamless Java integration.
what: Beyond the C reference implementation, several implementations exist for different platforms and goals (Jython on the JVM, IronPython on .NET, PyPy as a Python-written optimizing compiler, Stackless reducing C-stack reliance to enable co-routines, continuations and microthreads).

quote: For error handling, Python uses (non-resumable) exceptions.
what: Error handling is done through non-resumable exceptions, raised by a raise statement and handled by try/except/finally, with built-in operations throwing exceptions on error conditions.

quote: Although it is often viewed as a "scripting" language, it is really a general purpose programming language along the lines of Lisp or Smalltalk
what: Though often seen as a scripting language, Python is really a general purpose language in the lineage of Lisp or Smalltalk, usable across the whole range from throw-away scripts to large 24x7 web servers.

quote: This is no accident---the syntax of Python borrows heavily from C.
what: Python's surface syntax deliberately borrows heavily from C: keywords, identifier naming rules, and operator meanings are shared, so the resemblance to C or Pascal is no accident.

quote: ABC gave me the key inspiration for Python, Amoeba the immediate motivation, and the multimedia group fostered its growth
what: ABC gave the key inspiration for Python, Amoeba the immediate motivation, and the multimedia group its growth; Python is a direct product of this experience at CWI.

quote: Amoeba’s primitive operations were very different (and finer-grain) than the traditional primitive operations available in the Bourne shell
what: The decisive reason the Bourne shell wouldn't do was that Amoeba, as a distributed micro-kernel system with a radically new design, had primitive operations very different and finer-grained than those of the traditional shell.

quote: borrow everything I liked from ABC while at the same time fixing all its problems (as I perceived them)
what: The design program for Python was to keep what he liked from ABC while fixing the problems he perceived in it; the first problem he chose to fix was the name.

quote: there was a need for a language that would “bridge the gap between C and the shell.”  For a long time, this was Python’s main catchphrase.
what: Python's original motivation was the need for a higher-level language in the Amoeba project, because writing system administration utilities in C took too long and the Bourne shell wouldn't work; the aim was a language to bridge C and the shell.

quote: I decided to design a language of my own which would borrow everything I liked from ABC while at the same time fixing all its problems (as I perceived them)
what: Rather than port an existing language, van Rossum decided to design his own, because there weren't many suitable languages around; Perl 3 was even more tied to Unix than the Bourne shell.

quote: it fit in the tradition of naming languages after famous people, like Pascal, Ada, and Eiffel
what: "Python" was chosen as suitably irreverent for a skunkworks project, catchy and edgy, while still fitting the tradition of naming languages after famous people (Pascal, Ada, Eiffel) and the Amoeba group's habit of naming programs after TV shows.

quote: Python was open source before the term was even invented by Eric Raymond and Bruce Perens in late 1997
what: Python's first public release (0.9.0) used a license that was an almost verbatim copy of the X11 MIT license, so Python was open source before the term itself was coined.

quote: the first piece of code I wrote for Python’s implementation was a simple LL(1) parser generator I called “pgen." ... still part of the Python source distribution and probably the least changed of all the code
what: The first piece of code written for Python's implementation was a simple LL(1) parser generator, "pgen," which is still part of the source distribution and the least changed of all the code.

quote: There was immediately a lot of feedback and with this encouragement I kept a steady stream of releases coming for the next few years
what: Immediate feedback and encouragement led him to keep a steady stream of releases, adopting CVS to track changes and share coding responsibilities.

quote: For many years I resisted attempts to associate the language with snakes. I finally gave up when O’Reilly wanted to put a snake on the front of their first Python book
what: For many years he resisted associating the language with snakes, giving up only when O'Reilly's animal-cover tradition made a snake the cover of the first Python book.

quote: my tastes in programming language syntax were strongly influenced by languages like Algol 60, Pascal, Algol 68 ..., and last but not least, ABC
what: His tastes in programming-language syntax, which shaped his dislike of Perl's syntax, were strongly influenced by Algol 60, Pascal, Algol 68, and ABC.

quote: rather than over-analyzing the naming problem, I decided to under-analyze it. I picked the first thing that came to mind
what: Rather than over-analyzing the naming problem (as the ABC team had with "as simple as ABC"), he deliberately under-analyzed it and picked the first thing that came to mind, Monty Python.

quote: Jim would also author IronPython, the Python port to Microsoft's .NET
what: Van Rossum notes a further Python implementation, authored by Jim Hugunin, porting the language to Microsoft's .NET.

quote: the development of JPython (later shortened to Jython), a Python implementation in and for Java
what: A Python implementation written in and targeting Java, first created by Jim Hugunin, establishing that Python could be realized on a platform other than C.

quote: Bob Kahn, was the first to point out to me how much Python has in common with Lisp, despite being completely different at a superficial (syntactic) level
what: Van Rossum reports Bob Kahn's observation that Python has much in common with Lisp despite being completely different at the superficial, syntactic level, distinguishing a language's deep structure from its surface syntax.

quote: Python's first and foremost influence was ABC... It was designed by first doing a task analysis of the programming task and then doing several iterations that included serious user testing.
what: Python's first and foremost influence was ABC, a teaching language designed at CWI by first analyzing the programming task and then iterating with serious user testing; van Rossum's role was implementing the language and its editing environment.

quote: Feeling that there was still an important use case for unbounded exact numbers, I added a bignum data type, which I called long.
what: Feeling there was still a use case for unbounded exact numbers, he added a bignum type called long, reusing a bignum implementation left from an earlier unfinished attempt to improve ABC.

quote: ABC's authors did invent the use of the colon that separates the lead-in clause from the indented block. After early user testing without the colon, it was discovered that the meaning of the indentation was unclear to beginners... The addition of the colon clarified it significantly
what: ABC's authors invented the colon separating the lead-in clause from the indented block; user testing without it showed the indentation's meaning was unclear to beginners, and the colon clarified it by drawing attention to what follows and tying the phrases together.

open: he calls the approach "ugly but pragmatic"
quote: I settled for an ugly but pragmatic approach where a trailing comma would turn an expression into a one-tuple and \"()\" would represent a zero-tuple... I felt representing the empty tuple by \"nothing\" could too easily mask genuine typos.
what: Adding indexing forced resolving tuples of length 0 and 1; to keep the printed-repr rule yet not lose the distinction between a one-tuple and a parenthesized expression, he used a trailing comma for one-tuples and "()" for the empty tuple, requiring parentheses only there so that representing the empty tuple as nothing would not mask typos.

quote: This is one area where Python violated the ABC-inspired philosophy of not requiring users to care about a uninteresting implementation details.
what: Having two integer types forced a way to distinguish them; requiring a trailing L to mark longs violated the ABC-inspired philosophy of not making users care about uninteresting implementation details.

quote: I also replaced the sorted tables with a hash table implementation. I chose a hash table because I believed this to be faster and easier to implement than ABC's B-tree implementation.
what: He replaced ABC's sorted tables with a hash table, believing it faster and easier to implement than ABC's asymptotically optimal B-tree, which proved hard to implement correctly and sub-optimal for small sizes.

quote: Python's use of indentation comes directly from ABC, but this idea didn't originate with ABC--it had already been promoted by Donald Knuth and was a well-known concept of programming style.
what: Python's indentation comes from ABC, though the idea predates ABC (promoted by Knuth, used by occam); it is a well-known concept of programming style.

quote: A more egregious error was that my implementation of integers and longs had slightly different semantics in certain cases!
what: A more egregious error was that int and long had slightly different semantics: machine ints silently clipped on overflow and were treated as unsigned by bitwise, shift, and octal/hex conversions, while longs were always signed, so the same operation could differ by representation.

quote: So I changed the list type into a flexible array with insert and delete operations, giving users complete control over the ordering of items in a list. A sort method supported the occasional need for sorted results.
what: ABC's lists were sorted bags unsuitable for representing a sequence of lines read from a file, so van Rossum changed the list into a flexible array with insert and delete operations, giving users complete control over item ordering, with a sort method for occasional sorted results.

quote: I didn't want to use bignums for all integer operations... I envisioned machine integers being used for all of the most-common cases and the extra range of bignums only coming into play when doing \"serious math\"
what: Although he added bignums, he did not want them for all integer operations: profiling showed integer operations are a significant fraction of running time and the most common use is indexing sequences that fit in memory, so machine integers serve the common cases and bignums only "serious math."

quote: The rational numbers didn't pan out in my view... For Python I therefore chose a more traditional model with machine integers and machine binary floating point.
what: Numbers are where he strayed most from ABC: ABC's exact arbitrary-precision rationals didn't pan out (a tax computation ran on numbers with thousands of digits), so Python chose a traditional model of machine integers and binary floating point, represented by the C types long and double.

quote: I decided that there should be no undefined result values in Python – instead, exceptions should always be raised when no correct return value can be computed.
what: The positive lesson: there should be no undefined result values in Python; an exception is always raised when no correct value can be computed, so programs never fail from silently passed undefined values, a principle still held in the language and standard library.

quote: The extra cost of the overflow check would be dwarfed by the overhead I was already incurring due to the implementation choice of allocating a new object for the result.
what: A painful debugging of "Meertens numbers," whose intermediate results exceeded 32 bits, convinced him to check all integer operations for overflow; the extra cost was dwarfed by the overhead already incurred from allocating a new object for each result.

quote: I changed most arithmetic operations to raise an OverflowError exception when the result didn't fit... Had I not added this check, Python users would have undoubtedly started writing code that relied on the semantics of signed binary arithmetic modulo 2**32 (like C users do), and fixing the mistake would have been a much more painful transition to the community.
what: To resolve this he changed most arithmetic operations to raise OverflowError rather than silently clip (except bitwise operations, where C behavior was expected), reasoning that otherwise users would come to rely on signed modulo-2**32 semantics and fixing it later would be a painful transition.

quote: One of the rules I took from ABC was that every data type, when printed or converted to a string, should be represented by an expression that was a valid input to the language's parser.
what: A rule taken from ABC is that every data type, when printed or converted to a string, should be represented by an expression that is valid input to the parser.

quote: I decided to generalize these to a common concept, the sequence. This generalization made it so certain core operations such as getting the length (len(s)), indexing (s[i]), slicing (s[i:j]), and iteration (for i in s) worked the same on any sequence type.
what: Having three indexable types (list, tuple, string), he generalized them to a common concept, the sequence, so that length, indexing, slicing, and iteration work the same on any sequence type.

open: the same C rule "T returns T" also caused the integer-division truncation mistake, discussed in a later post
quote: In hindsight, I should have made integer operations that overflow promote their result to longs. This is the way that Python works today, but it took a long time to make this transition.
what: Raising an overflow exception was still not right; stuck on C's rule that operations on type T return type T, he should have had overflowing integer operations promote their result to longs, as Python does today, though the transition took a long time.

quote: I kept ABC's immutable tuple data type... Since tuples are internally represented by arrays, I decided to add array-like indexing and slicing.
what: He kept ABC's immutable tuple (with packing and unpacking taken directly from ABC) and, since tuples are internally arrays, added array-like indexing and slicing.

quote: ABC doesn't ... exclusively rely on static type checking to keep the program from crashing, but has a run-time library that checks the argument types for all operations again each time they are executed.
what: ABC did not rely only on static checking; its run-time library re-checked argument types on every operation, so the gap between ABC and Python is smaller than it seems.

quote: ABC uses dynamic type checking for global variables, but static type checking for local variables. To simplify the implementation, local variables are dynamically type checked as well.
what: ABC compromised by using dynamic type checking for global variables and static checking for local ones, though to simplify implementation local variables were dynamically checked as well.

quote: ABC is statically typed which meant that the ABC compiler analyzes the use of types in a program and decides whether they are used consistently. If not, the program is rejected ... ABC used type inference (not unlike Haskell) instead of explicit type declarations
what: ABC was statically typed, rejecting inconsistent programs before execution, and unlike most statically typed languages of its time used type inference rather than explicit declarations, like Haskell rather than C.

quote: once you decide on dynamic typing, there is no way to go back. ABC’s built-in operations were carefully designed so that the type of the arguments could be deduced from the form of the operation ... In Python, such deductions cannot generally be made.
what: Once dynamic typing is chosen there is no going back, because ABC's operations were designed so argument types could be deduced from the form of the operation, while in Python such deductions generally cannot be made.

quote: the most important reason why ABC has run time type checking in addition to static type checking is that it is interactive.
what: The most important reason ABC had run-time type checking is that it is interactive: across separately entered statements it is unreasonable to forbid reusing a variable name with a different type.

quote: the expression “x+y” could be a string concatenation, a numeric addition, or an overloaded operation on user-defined types.
what: In Python an expression like "x+y" is ambiguous between string concatenation, numeric addition, or an overloaded operation on user-defined types, so the type cannot be deduced from the operation's form.

quote: Python simply drops the compile-time type checking completely. This is entirely in line with Python’s “corner-cutting” philosophy as it’s a simplification of the implementation that does not affect the eventual safety, since all type errors are caught at run time
what: Python's approach is a small step from ABC's: it drops compile-time type checking completely, in line with Python's "corner-cutting" philosophy, a simplification that does not affect safety since all type errors are still caught at run time before the interpreter can malfunction.

quote: In contrast, Python is dynamically typed.  The Python compiler is blissfully unaware of the types used in a program, and all type checking is done at run time.
what: Python is dynamically typed: the compiler ignores the types in a program and all type checking happens at run time, in contrast to ABC's static typing.

quote: This was done in part as a sanity check for the compiler’s type-checking algorithms ... The runtime library was also useful as a debugging aid since explicit run time type checking could produce nice error messages ... instead of the core dumps
what: ABC's run-time type checking served as a sanity check for the compiler's not-fully-implemented type-checking algorithms and as a debugging aid producing readable error messages instead of core dumps.

quote: Users are often surprised to learn that any sequence of valid Python statements can appear in a class body. This capability was really just a straightforward extension of my desire to keep the syntax simple as well as not artificially limiting what might possibly be useful.
what: Because the class body is just executed statements, any valid Python statements may appear in it, which surprises users; this followed from keeping the syntax simple and not artificially limiting what might be useful.

quote: Changing the semantics of assignment to assign to an instance variable if one already existed and to a local otherwise wouldn't work either, since this would create a bootstrap problem: how does an instance variable get created initially?
what: Changing assignment to target an existing instance variable and otherwise a local fails too, because of a bootstrap problem: there would be no way for an instance variable to be created the first time.

quote: Python's assignment doesn't search for the variable name in the dictionaries, but simply adds or replaces the variable in the first dictionary in the search order, normally the local variables... making the instance dictionary the first item in the search order would make it impossible to assign to local variables in a method.
what: Variable reference searches locals, globals, built-ins in order, but assignment does not search: it always creates or replaces in the first dictionary (locals), with a per-variable global declaration as the only override. This is why putting the instance dictionary first breaks assignment to locals, and swapping the order merely reverses the problem.

quote: Whenever changes are made to instance or class variables, those changes are simply reflected in the underlying dictionary object... lookups are performed in the class dictionary and then in the class dictionaries of each of the base classes.
what: The mechanics are plain dictionary operations: setting a variable updates the instance dictionary; a lookup checks the instance dictionary, then the class dictionary, then the base classes' dictionaries.

quote: Python is implemented in C as a classic stack-based byte code interpreter or "virtual machine" along with a collection of primitive types also implemented in C. The underlying architecture uses "objects" throughout, but since C has no direct support for objects, they are implemented using structures and function pointers.
what: Python is a stack-based bytecode interpreter written in C, with primitive types in C; objects are built from C structures and function pointers because C has no direct object support.

quote: making the class object itself callable was the right, "minimal" solution, requiring no new syntax... what I had done was simply to turn each class into its own factory.
what: Unlike C++ and Java's "new" operator, Python makes the class object itself callable for instantiation, the minimal solution requiring no new syntax, since the parser does not care what kind of object is called; each class is thereby its own factory, anticipating the later factory-function pattern.

quote: it made sense to me to simply interpret the class body as a series of statements that were executed in a new namespace. The dictionary of this namespace would then be captured and used to initialize the class dictionary and create a class object.
what: To reuse existing code, the class body is interpreted as statements executed in a new namespace; its resulting dictionary of locals initializes the class dictionary. Concretely the body becomes an anonymous function returning its local dictionary, passed to a helper that creates the class object, which is then bound to the class name in the surrounding scope.

quote: the set of methods of a class were stored in a dictionary whose keys are the method names. This, I dubbed the class dictionary.
what: The class object holds what is shared across instances, chiefly methods, in a "class dictionary" keyed by method name; again the simplest possible design.

quote: there was no inherent reason why other kinds of objects couldn't be placed there as well. Thus, if objects such as integers or strings are stored in the class dictionary, they become what are known as class variables
what: Because the class dictionary can hold any object, storing non-method objects there yields class variables, shared by all instances; this feature falls out of the design rather than being designed in.

quote: classes were added late during Python's first year of development at CWI, though well before the first public release
what: Classes were not part of Python's earliest design; they were added late in the first year of development at CWI, yet before the first public release.

open: the later, more sophisticated MRO is deferred to a later blog and not described here
quote: This is commonly referred to as the depth-first, left-to-right rule, and has been the default method resolution order (MRO) used in most versions of Python. More modern releases have adapted a more sophisticated MRO
what: Method resolution walks the class dictionary then each base class recursively, stopping at the first hit: the depth-first, left-to-right rule, the default MRO in most versions of Python.

quote: I decided that these features could be handled by simply requiring the user to implement methods with special names such as __init__, __del__, and so forth. This naming convention was taken from C where identifiers starting with underscores are reserved by the compiler and often have special meaning
what: Rather than new syntax for special class methods like initializers and destructors, the user implements methods with special names such as __init__ and __del__; the underscore convention was taken from C, where leading-underscore identifiers are reserved and often special (e.g. __FILE__).

quote: it also makes it possible to modify a class dynamically... methods can be added or modified by simply updating the class dictionary after a class object has already been created!... individual objects can be modified dynamically by adding, modifying, and deleting instance variables
what: The simple implementation makes classes first-class, introspectable objects and allows dynamic modification: methods added or changed by updating the class dictionary take immediate effect on all instances and subclasses; instances too can gain, change or lose variables.

quote: With explicit references, there is no need to have a special syntax for method definitions nor do you have to worry about complicated semantics concerning variable lookup. Instead, one simply defines a function whose first argument corresponds to the instance, which by convention is named "self."
what: With explicit references, no special method-definition syntax and no complicated variable-lookup semantics are needed: a method is just a function whose first argument, by convention named "self," is the instance.

quote: I decided to make such explicit references the only way to reference instance variables... rather than making the current object ("this") a special keyword, I would simply make "this" (or its equivalent) the first named argument to a method. Instance variables would just always be referenced as attributes of that argument.
what: The author gave up implicit instance-variable references and made explicit reference the only way, following C++'s this->foo; rather than making the current object a keyword, he made it the first named argument to a method, so instance variables are always attributes of that argument.

quote: it quickly became clear that such an approach would be impossible because there was no way to elegantly distinguish instance variables from local variables in a language without variable declarations.
what: The author first hoped to emulate C++'s implicit instance variables, where a method's unqualified reference resolves to the instance variable; this proved impossible in a language without variable declarations, since instance and local variables could not be elegantly distinguished.

quote: I settled on the simplest possible design; a scheme where objects were represented by a new kind of built-in object that stored a class reference pointing to a "class object" shared by all instances of the same class, and a dictionary, dubbed the "instance dictionary", that contained the instance variables.
what: The chosen design for user-defined objects is the simplest possible: an instance is a built-in object holding a class reference and an "instance dictionary" of instance variables.

quote: This approach resembles something I had seen in Modula-3, which had already provided me with the syntax for import and exception handling... calling x.m(args) is equivalent to calling f(x, args). This matches the typical implementation of objects and methods
what: The self approach resembles Modula-3, which also gave Python its import and exception-handling syntax; Modula-3's record types hold function-pointer members with sugar so that x.m(args) equals f(x, args), matching the typical object implementation and letting instance variables equate to attributes of the first argument.

quote: a feature that I later learned made Python's implementation of objects more permissive than that found in Smalltalk which restricts the set of attributes to those specified at the time of object creation
what: Python's objects are more permissive than Smalltalk's, which restricts an object's attributes to those fixed at creation; the author learned this only later.

quote: as long as I was going to support inheritance, I might as well support a simple-minded version of multiple inheritance. Thus, every class object could have one or more base classes.
what: Class objects store references to base classes for inheritance; being naïve about classes but aware of C++'s recent multiple inheritance, the author supported a simple-minded multiple inheritance since he was adding inheritance anyway.

quote: Eventually, new-style classes made it necessary to control changes to the class __dict__; you can still dynamically modify a class, but you must use attribute assignment rather than using the class __dict__ directly.
what: New-style classes later required controlling changes to a class's __dict__: a class can still be modified dynamically, but through attribute assignment rather than by using the class __dict__ directly.

quote: Python performs no advanced error checking or conformance checking when locating methods... no checks are performed to make sure that the redefined method has the same number of arguments... The above method resolution algorithm merely returns the first method found and calls it with whatever arguments the user has supplied.
what: To keep things simple, method lookup does no error or conformance checking; an overriding method need not match the base method's arguments, and the first method found is called with whatever arguments the user supplied.

quote: A major design constraint was that I didn't want to add syntax for methods that differed from the syntax for functions. Refactoring the grammar and the byte code generator to handle such similar cases differently felt like a huge task.
what: A major design constraint was to not add a method syntax different from function syntax, because refactoring the grammar and bytecode generator to treat the similar cases differently felt like a huge task.

open: the author marks the attribution as a belief ("I believe")
quote: I believe my colleague Siebren van der Zee was the first to suggest that Python should allow class definitions similar to those in C++ so that objects could also be implemented in Python.
what: Siebren van der Zee suggested Python should allow class definitions like C++ so that objects could be implemented in Python, not only in C; this motivated user-defined classes.

quote: Requiring a special specification for instance variables, on the other hand, would have to be used almost everywhere in a class. Another possible solution would have been to make instance variables lexically distinct... Neither of these appealed to me (and they still don't).
what: Requiring explicit instance-variable declarations was rejected because the author had gotten this far with no declarations and they would be needed almost everywhere in a class; lexically distinct instance variables (a sigil like Ruby's @, or a naming convention) also did not appeal to him, then or now.

quote: I mapped the various function pointers to special method names such as __getattr__, __add__, and __call__. There is a direct correspondence between these names and the tables of function pointers one has to define when implementing new Python objects in C.
what: The special-method technique also lets user classes redefine Python's operators: the C-level function pointers (get attribute, add, call) are mapped to special method names (__getattr__, __add__, __call__), with a direct correspondence to the function-pointer tables defined when implementing objects in C.

quote: An object type is then represented by a statically allocated structure containing a series of function pointers, one for each standard operation... some operations are optional, and the object type may leave the function pointer NULL if it chooses not to implement that operation. In this case, the virtual machine either generates a run-time error or, in some cases, provides a default implementation
what: An object type is a statically allocated structure of function pointers, one per standard operation; optional operations may be left NULL, in which case the VM errors or supplies a default.

quote: Python's unique approach to introspection comes from its ability to make the type structure itself available at run-time as an object like all others.
what: Python's introspection comes from making the type structure itself available at run-time as an object like any other.

quote: the execution of that statement actually occurs in two steps.  First, a lookup of "a.spam" occurs.  This returns a bound method--a callable object.    Next, a function call operation "()" is applied to that object to invoke the method
what: Bound/unbound methods are central to how classes work: "a.spam()" executes in two steps, a lookup of "a.spam" returning a bound method, then a call "()" applied to that object.

quote: a different callable object known as a "bound method." is used. ... this wrapper implicitly stores the original instance that was used to obtain the method.
what: For a method obtained through an instance, a "bound method" wrapper implicitly stores the original instance so a later call sets it as the first argument.

quote: All of Python's objects were based on a common C data structure that was used everywhere in the interpreter. ... it just didn't matter if the structure happened to represent a simple object such as an integer or something more complicated such as a class.
what: The implementation made first-class-everything simple because all Python objects were based on one common C data structure used everywhere in the interpreter, regardless of whether it held an integer or a class.

quote: One of my goals for Python was to make it so that all objects were "first class."  By this, I meant that I wanted all objects that could be named in the language ... to have equal status.
what: Guido's goal that every object nameable in Python (integers, strings, functions, classes, modules, methods) have equal status: assignable to variables, placed in lists, stored in dictionaries, passed as arguments.

quote: there was still one subtle aspect of classes that I still needed to address---namely, the problem of making methods first class objects.
what: A subtle aspect of making the idea complete was making methods first-class objects, since a method, unlike an ordinary function, expects its first argument to be an instance of its class.

quote: the same internal object type is used to represent bound and unbound methods.   One of the attributes of this object contains a reference to an instance.   If set to None, the method is unbound.  Otherwise, the method is bound.
what: Bound and unbound methods are the same internal object type, distinguished by an instance attribute: None means unbound, otherwise bound.

quote: I created a type of callable object known as an "unbound method."   An unbound method was really just a thin wrapper around the function object that implemented a method, but it enforced a restriction that the first argument had to be an instance of the class in which the method was defined.
what: Guido created a callable object, the "unbound method," a thin wrapper around the function that enforced the restriction that the first argument be an instance of the class in which the method was defined.

quote: In Python 3000, the concept of unbound methods has been removed ... the restriction that the first argument had to be an instance of A was rarely helpful in diagnosing problems, and frequently an obstacle to advanced usages
what: In Python 3000 unbound methods were removed and "A.spam" returns a plain function, because the first-argument restriction was rarely helpful for diagnosing problems and often obstructed advanced usages ("duck typing self").

quote: Rather than defining the class body as a series of function declarations only, it seemed to make sense to also allow regular variable assignments there. However, if I was going to allow that, why not go one step further and allow arbitrary executable code?
what: The reasoning began with allowing regular variable assignments in a class body, not just function declarations, then extended to allowing arbitrary executable code anywhere.

quote: grammar elements that had a “declarative flavor”, like import statements and function definitions, were allowed only at the top level in a module or script ... However, at the time I was adding support for classes, I decided that this was too restrictive.
what: In a very early version of the grammar, declarative-flavored elements like import statements and function definitions were allowed only at the top level of a module or script; adding classes, van Rossum judged this too restrictive.

quote: every part of the language is an executable statement, including function and class definitions.  That means that any statement can appear anywhere in a program.
what: Every part of Python is an executable statement, including function and class definitions, so any statement can appear anywhere in a program.

quote: the Python grammar technically allowed users to write things such as nested functions even though the underlying semantics of Python didn't support nested scopes. ... many of these "broken" features have been fixed. quote: this enabled a simplification of the grammar, since now all uses of statements (whether indented or not) could share the same grammar rule, and hence the compiler could use the same byte code generation function for all of them.

quote: The main reason however is that I worried about name clashes between unrelated exceptions defined in different modules. quote: In 1997, with Python 1.5, I introduced class exceptions into the language. Although class exceptions have been the recommended approach ever since, string exceptions were still supported for use by certain legacy applications through Python 2.5. They were finally removed in Python 2.6.
what: In 1997 with Python 1.5 he introduced class exceptions, the recommended approach since; string exceptions stayed for legacy use through Python 2.5 and were removed in 2.6.

quote: Early Python users discovered that within the same module, the byte code compiler would unify string literals ... it only worked for code defined in the same module---if one tried to catch exceptions using the exception error message in a different module, it broke mysteriously. what: In practice the byte code compiler unified string literals within a module, so by accident exceptions could be caught by the error-message literal as well as the name; this worked only within a module and broke mysteriously across modules, causing widespread confusion.

quote: In early Python however, I chose to identify exceptions by strings. This was unfortunate, but I had two reasons for taking this approach. First, I learned about exceptions from Modula-3, where exceptions are unique tokens. Second, I introduced exceptions before I introduced user-defined classes.
what: In early Python the author identified exceptions by strings, which he judges unfortunate, for two reasons: he learned exceptions from Modula-3 (where they are unique tokens), and he introduced exceptions before user-defined classes existed.

quote: In modern languages (including modern Python :-), exceptions are defined in terms of user-defined classes.
what: In modern languages, and in modern Python, exceptions are defined by user-defined classes.

quote: Early on, I knew I wanted Python to use exceptions for error handling.
what: From the start the author wanted Python to handle errors through exceptions.

quote: I chose semantics where different string objects would represent different exceptions, even if they had the same value ... The idea was that exceptions would always be referenced by their name, which would imply object identity, never by their value, which would require string equality.
what: He chose semantics where distinct string objects are distinct exceptions even with equal value, so exceptions are referenced by name (object identity) and never by value (string equality), keeping exceptions in different modules independent.

quote: (This was also long before certain string literals would be automatically be “interned”.)
what: This design predated the automatic interning of certain string literals.

quote: This approach was influenced by Modula-3’s exceptions, where each exception declaration creates a unique “exception token” that can’t be confused with any other exception token.
what: The design was influenced by Modula-3, where each exception declaration creates a unique token that can't be confused with another.

quote: I think I also wanted to optimize testing for exceptions by using pointer comparisons instead of string value comparisons in a misguided attempt to prematurely optimize execution time (a rare one – I usually optimized for my own coding time!).
what: He also wanted to test exceptions by pointer comparison rather than string value comparison, which he now calls a misguided premature optimization of execution time, rare for him since he usually optimized his own coding time.

quote: as every built-in object type required a considerable coding effort in C, I decided to reuse an existing built-in type. And, since exceptions are associated with error messages, it seemed natural to use strings to represent exceptions.
what: A new built-in object type for exceptions would have cost considerable C coding, so he reused an existing built-in type; strings seemed natural because exceptions carry error messages.

quote: a critical part of making exceptions work is to come up with some kind of scheme for identifying different kinds of exceptions.
what: Making exceptions work requires some scheme for distinguishing one kind of exception from another.

quote: in ABC, when you divided two integers, the result was an exact rational number representing the result.  In Python however, integer division truncated the result to an integer.
what: In ABC, dividing two integers gave an exact rational number; in Python integer division truncated instead.

quote: with Python, I relied on the other numerical model with which I was familiar, C. ... I chose to represent Python integers by a C long (guaranteeing at least 32 bits of precision) and floating point numbers by a C double.   I then added an arbitrary precision integer type which I called \"long.\"
what: For Python he relied on C's numerical model: ints as a C long of at least 32 bits, floats as a C double, plus an arbitrary precision integer type called "long".

quote: passing an integer can cause an answer that is close to the correct answer but has a much larger error – which is difficult to debug or even notice.
what: Passing an integer where a float is expected yields an answer close to correct but with much larger error, hard to debug or notice, unlike an invalid type such as a string which is caught quickly (multiplication being the exception).

quote: A truncating division operator (//) was added to the language to provide the same functionality.   In addition, a mechanism (\"from __future__ import division\") was introduced by which the new integer division semantics could be enabled. ... the correct behavior has become the default behavior in Python 3000.
what: Fixing integer division was hard because programs relied on truncation; the fix was a truncating operator (//), a per-module opt-in ("from __future__ import division"), and a command line flag (-Qxxx), with the correct behavior becoming the default in Python 3000.

quote: I initially used another misguided rule that forbade mixed-mode arithmetic, with the aim of making the type implementations independent from each other. ... what: He initially forbade mixed-mode arithmetic to keep the type implementations independent, so one couldn't add an int to a float or even an int to a long; Tim Peters convinced him this was a bad idea and he introduced mixed-mode arithmetic with the usual coercion rules.

quote: the proposal to change this has had some tough opposition from folks who believed that learning about integer division was one of the more useful \"rites of passage\" for all programmers.
what: Proposals to change integer division met opposition from those who held that learning integer division was a useful "rite of passage" for programmers.

quote: Python's handling of integer division is an example of early mistake with huge consequences.   As mentioned earlier, when Python was created, I abandoned the approach to numbers that had been used in ABC.
what: Guido names Python's truncating integer division as an early design mistake with large consequences, and notes he abandoned ABC's approach to numbers when he created Python.

quote: since Python doesn’t have type declarations, nothing is there to stop a caller from providing you with integer arguments. In a statically typed language, like C, the compiler will coerce the arguments to floats, but Python does no such thing
what: Because Python has no type declarations, nothing stops a caller from passing integers to an algorithm meant for floats; unlike statically typed C, Python does not coerce the arguments, so the algorithm runs with integers until mixed-mode arithmetic yields floats.

open: whether the problem was inherent to rationals or to how beginners met them is left as experience, not settled.
quote: In my experience, rational numbers didn't pan out as ABC's designers had hoped.
what: Exact rational numbers didn't work out as ABC's designers hoped: programs silently used rationals with thousands of digits of precision, running slow, and the fix (starting with an inexact zero) was non-intuitive and hard to debug for beginners.

quote: The major mistake was that I also borrowed a rule that makes sense in C but not so much in a very-high-level language. For the standard arithmetic operations, including division, the result would always be the same type as the operands.
what: The major mistake was borrowing C's rule that an arithmetic operation's result is always the same type as its operands, a rule that makes sense in C but not in a very-high-level language.

quote: when division is involved, and the possibility exists that both operands are integers, the numeric result is silently truncated, essentially inserting a potentially large error into the computation.
what: Since integers behave like floats for everything except division, one is misled to expect algorithms to behave the same either way; but with two integer operands division silently truncates, inserting a potentially large error, and defensive coercion is tedious, hurts readability and maintainability, and blocks use with complex arguments.
