quote: Instead of hard-coding the behavior that Python function objects are wrapped and other objects aren’t, the wrapping is now left up to the object found by the attribute search ... If the object found by an attribute search happens to have a special method named __get__, it is considered to be a \"descriptor\" object.
what: Python 2.2 generalized the wrapping behavior: instead of hard-coding which objects get wrapped, the object found by the attribute search decides via a `__get__` method; function objects gained a `__get__` so users can define their own descriptor classes.

quote: Thus, by redefining these methods, a descriptor object can have complete control over what it means to get, set, and delete an attribute. However, it's important emphasize that this customization only applies when a descriptor instance appears in a class dictionary—not the instance dictionary of an object.
what: The same idea was extended to setting and deleting attributes through `__set__` and `__delete__`, giving a descriptor complete control over get/set/delete; this customization applies only when the descriptor appears in a class dictionary, not an instance dictionary.

quote: Descriptors are a generalization of the concept of bound methods, which was central to the implementation of classic classes.
what: Descriptors generalize the concept of bound methods, which was central to classic classes; in classic classes a function found in a class dictionary during attribute lookup was returned as a currying wrapper that inserts the instance in front of the argument list.

quote: One limitation was that it was prevented the creation of “hybrid” classes that had some methods implemented in Python and others in C, because only Python functions were being wrapped in such a way as to provide the method with access to the instance, and this behavior was hard-coded in the language.
what: The old scheme only wrapped Python function objects and this was hard-coded, preventing "hybrid" classes mixing Python and C methods and giving no obvious way to define other kinds of methods such as static member functions.

quote: By overriding __new__() a class author can implement patterns like the Singleton Pattern, return a previously created instance (e.g., from a free list), or to return an instance of a different class (e.g., a subclass).
what: Overriding `__new__()` lets a class implement patterns like Singleton, return a previously created instance, or return an instance of a different class; it is also used in pickle to create instances while unserializing without invoking `__init__`.

quote: Another use of __new__ is to help with the subclassing of immutable types. By the nature of their immutability, these kinds of objects can not be initialized through a standard __init__() method.
what: Immutable objects cannot be initialized through a standard `__init__()`, so `__new__` lets their subclasses perform any special initialization as the object is created, e.g. passing a modified value to the base class `__new__`.

quote: Old-style classes never really provided a hook for customizing the creation of objects although there were library modules allowed certain kinds of objects to be created in non-standard ways (e.g., the \"new\" module).
what: Old-style classes gave `__init__()` for initializing an instance after creation but never provided a real hook to customize how instances are created; `__new__()` was introduced as a class method so the author can control instance creation.

quote: On the surface, new-style classes appear very similar to the original class implementation. However, new-style classes also introduced a number of new concepts:
what: New-style classes look similar to the original class implementation on the surface, but introduced several new concepts: `__new__()`, descriptors, static and class methods, properties, decorators, slots, and a new Method Resolution Order.

quote: At the time, it was deemed too controversial to simultaneously introduce a major new feature along with new syntax (which always leads to a heated debate).
what: These descriptors were introduced without special syntax because it was deemed too controversial to add a major feature and new syntax at once; users wrapped methods with extra assignment statements instead.

quote: This is the fundamental mechanism by which methods in classes obtain their \"self\" argument.
what: The wrapper returned by attribute lookup is the fundamental mechanism by which methods obtain their "self" argument, calling the original function with the instance inserted in front.

quote: Another enhancement made possible with descriptors was the introduction of the __slots__ attribute on classes.
what: `__slots__` is another application of descriptors: it restricts valid attribute names, removes the instance `__dict__`, and stores attributes in array locations, each slot being a descriptor that gets/sets via an array index, implemented entirely in C.

open: The performance fear turned out unnecessary ("This turned out unnecessary"), yet `__slots__` remained because it was too late to remove it.
quote: Some people mistakenly assume that the intended purpose of __slots__ is to increase code safety (by restricting the attribute names). In reality, my ultimate goal was performance.
what: Contrary to the assumption that `__slots__` is for code safety, its ultimate goal was performance; Guido feared the class-system changes (the extra data-descriptor check on every attribute access) would hurt performance, so `__slots__` was a fallback optimization. It turned out unnecessary but was too late to remove, though used properly it can reduce memory footprint.

quote: In other words, x.f(0) is equivalent to C.f(x, 0). This is a pretty fundamental equivalence in Python.
what: Asking the class for the function attribute returns the unwrapped function, so `x.f(0)` is equivalent to `C.f(x, 0)`, a fundamental equivalence in Python.

quote: The antigravity module, referencing the XKCD comic mentioning Python, was added to Python 3 by Skip Montanaro.
what: Python 3's standard library carries an easter egg module, `antigravity`, referencing the XKCD comic that mentions Python; its inclusion is treated as a deliberate playful element of the distribution rather than functional code. Van Rossum reports it was added to Python 3 by Skip Montanaro and originated as a launch easter egg in Google App Engine.

quote: The Python 3 stdlib version has an easter egg inside the easter egg, ... it defines a function that purports to implement the XKCD geohashing algorithm.
what: The stdlib version nests a second hidden joke in its source: a function that purports to implement the XKCD geohashing algorithm, so the playfulness is layered for anyone who reads the code.

quote: it was decided that the MRO adopted for Python 2.2 was broken and that Python should adopt the C3 Linearization algorithm described in the paper \"A Monotonic Superclass Linearization for Dylan\"
what: After discussion it was decided to replace the 2.2 scheme with the academically published C3 Linearization algorithm from the Dylan paper.

quote: Python will now reject any inheritance hierarchy that has an inconsistent ordering of base classes.
what: A consequence of adopting C3 is that Python now rejects any inheritance hierarchy with an inconsistent ordering of base classes rather than resolving it silently.

quote: when looking up a method, base classes were searched using a simple depth-first left-to-right scheme.   The first matching object found during this search would be returned.
what: Classic classes resolved methods by a simple depth-first, left-to-right search, returning the first match found.

quote: This scheme works fine for simple cases, but has problems that become apparent when one considers more complicated uses of multiple inheritance.  One problem concerns method lookup under \"diamond inheritance.\"
what: The classic depth-first scheme works for simple cases but breaks under diamond inheritance, where it finds the shared ancestor's method instead of the more specialized override.

quote: This is what I implemented for Python 2.2, but I documented the earlier algorithm (naïvely thinking it didn't matter much).
what: Van Rossum implemented one algorithm for 2.2 but documented the earlier simpler one, thinking the difference did not matter much; a regret.

quote: if you write down all of the ordering rules imposed by inheritance relationships in a complex class hierarchy, the algorithm will determine a monotonic ordering of the classes that satisfies all of them.   If such an ordering can not be determined, the algorithm will fail.
what: Each inheritance relationship imposes simple ordering rules (a subclass before its base; earlier-listed bases before later ones), and C3 finds a monotonic ordering satisfying all of them or fails.

quote: if you have already determined that class A should be checked before class B, then you should never encounter a situation that requires class B to be checked before class A (otherwise, the result is undefined and the inheritance hierarchy should be rejected).
what: The core defect of the 2.2 algorithm was monotonicity: once A is determined to precede B, no later rule should force B before A, or the hierarchy is undefined and should be rejected.

quote: the order in which base classes are searched when looking for a method is often called the Method Resolution Order, or MRO. (In Python this also applies to other attributes.)
what: In languages with multiple inheritance, the Method Resolution Order (MRO) is the order base classes are searched for a method; in Python it also governs lookup of other attributes.

quote: there was a special case to deal with a situation when two bases classes occurred in a different order in the inheritance list of two different derived classes ... this algorithm tried to preserve the order of classes for bases that appeared first in the search process.
what: The real 2.2 algorithm added a special case that reordered bases to preserve the order in which classes first appeared in the search, departing from the documented algorithm.

quote: For languages that support single inheritance only, the MRO is uninteresting; but when multiple inheritance comes into play, the choice of an MRO algorithm can be remarkably subtle.
what: MRO only becomes an interesting and subtle problem once multiple inheritance is in play; under single inheritance it is uninteresting.

quote: Although this kind of multiple inheritance was rare in existing code, new-style classes would make it commonplace.   This is because all new-style classes were defined by inheriting from a base class object.
what: Because all new-style classes inherit from a common base object, every use of multiple inheritance creates a diamond, turning a rare problem into a commonplace one.

quote: since object defined a number of methods that are sometimes extended by subtypes (e.g., __setattr__()), the resolution order becomes critical.
what: Since object defines methods that subtypes sometimes extend (e.g. __setattr__), the resolution order becomes critical so the subtype's override applies.

quote: Samuele Pedroni discovered an inconsistency between the documented MRO algorithm and the results that were actually observed in real-code.   Moreover, inconsistencies were occurring even in code that did not fall under the special case observed above.
what: Samuele Pedroni found that the actual behavior diverged from the documented algorithm, and that inconsistencies arose even outside the known special case, leading to the judgment that the 2.2 MRO was broken.

quote: I adopted a scheme where the MRO would be pre-computed when a class was defined and stored as an attribute of each class object. ... If any class was duplicated in this search, all but the last occurrence would be deleted from the MRO list.
what: For Python 2.2 the MRO was pre-computed at class-definition time and stored as an attribute of the class object, dropping all but the last occurrence of a duplicated class.

quote: Python has known at least three different MRO algorithms: classic, Python 2.2 new-style, and Python 2.3 new-style (a.k.a. C3). Only the latter survives in Python 3.
what: Python has used three MRO algorithms over time (classic, 2.2 new-style, 2.3 new-style / C3), of which only C3 remains in Python 3.

quote: This, of course, matches the Zen of Python's \"errors should never pass silently\" rule.
what: Rejecting inconsistent hierarchies is aligned with the Zen of Python's rule that errors should never pass silently.

quote: one can argue that the redefined method C.save() is actually the method that you want to call, since it can be viewed as being \"more specialized\" than the method in A ... if the save() method is being used to save the state of an object, not calling C.save() would break the program since the state of C would be ignored.
what: When a subclass redefines a method inherited through a diamond, the more specialized redefinition is the one that should be called; otherwise the subclass's state is ignored and the program breaks.

open: a wish that Python for-loops could iterate over multiple sequences as Algol-60's step-until could: "In retrospect it would have been cool if Python for-loops had the ability to iterate over multiple sequences as well. Alas..." (line 32)
quote: This also reminded me of Algol-60, where you can write: for i := 1, 2, 3 do Statement
what: The bare comma-separated for-loop reminded Guido of Algol-60's for-loop form.

quote: if you wanted to loop over a bunch of known values, you shouldn't be bothered with having to put parentheses around them.
what: The original explicit for-loop had no ambiguity after 'in' because a colon always followed, so Guido decided looping over known values shouldn't require parentheses.

open: nested for-clauses are allowed but "rarely used though, since it typically maps a multi-dimensional entity to a one-dimensional list" (line 8).
quote: [f(x) for x in S if P(x)] This produces a list containing the values of the sequence S selected by the predicate P and mapped by the function f.
what: The chosen Python notation produces a list of the values of a sequence, selected by an optional predicate and mapped by a function, with multiple for-clauses allowed for nested loops.

quote: the list comprehension executes much faster ... because calling a lambda function creates a new stack frame while the expression in the list comprehension is evaluated without creating a new stack frame.
what: Comprehensions run faster than map+lambda because a lambda call creates a new stack frame while the comprehension's expression is evaluated without one.

quote: List comprehensions provide an alternative to using the built-in map() and filter() functions.
what: List comprehensions are an alternative to map() and filter(); on toy cases map/filter look more compact, but on realistic cases the comprehension wins.

quote: The factors affecting the design were backwards compatibility, avoiding ambiguity, the desire for equivalence, and evolution of the language.
what: Four factors governed the design of these notations: backwards compatibility, avoiding ambiguity, the desire for equivalence, and evolution of the language.

quote: a similar notation that represents a sequence of results without turning it into a concrete list. The new feature is called a "generator expression".
what: Generator expressions, added in 2.4 and enabled by generators, represent a sequence of results without building a concrete list, saving memory for large collections.

quote: the parentheses around a generator expression are not technically part of the generator expression syntax ... there would be two interpretations
what: The parentheses around a generator expression belong to the surrounding call, not to the genexp syntax, so a bare comma sequence after 'in' would have two interpretations.

quote: Generator expressions are implemented using generators, whose execution requires a separate execution frame. Thus, generator expressions ... were less efficient than list comprehensions.
what: Generator expressions cannot leak the variable because they run in a separate execution frame, which made them less efficient than list comprehensions in Python 2.

quote: in Python 2, this is a valid list comprehension: ... However this is not a valid generator expression
what: In Python 2 a list comprehension could take a bare comma sequence after 'in', but a generator expression could not, requiring parentheses.

quote: It has been argued that the real problem here is that Python's lambda notation is too verbose ... Personally, I disagree—I find the list comprehension notation much easier to read than the functional notation
what: Some argue the real problem is that lambda is too verbose and a terser anonymous-function syntax would make map() more attractive; Guido disagrees, preferring the comprehension's readability as expression complexity grows.

quote: they are a Pythonic interpretation of a well-known notation for sets used by mathematicians
what: List comprehensions are a Pythonic interpretation of the mathematical set-builder notation.

quote: we wanted the list comprehension ... to be fully equivalent to the following expansion using the built-in list() function applied to a generator expression ... Thus we decided to use the slightly more restrictive syntax of generator expressions for list comprehensions as well.
what: In Python 3 they decided a list comprehension should be fully equivalent to list() applied to the corresponding generator expression, so they gave list comprehensions the stricter genexp syntax.

quote: the list comprehension "leaks" the loop control variable into the surrounding scope ... It started out as an intentional compromise to make list comprehensions blindingly fast ... it definitely stung people occasionally.
what: In Python 2 a list comprehension leaks its loop control variable into the surrounding scope, an artifact of the original implementation, an intentional compromise for speed that occasionally stung people.

quote: In math, this form implies a universal set that is understood by the reader ... In Python, there is no concept of a universal set, and in Python 2.0, there were no sets.
what: The mathematical set-builder form implies a universal set understood from context; Python has no such concept, and at the time (2.0) no sets at all, which forced a different notation.

quote: both list comprehensions and generator expressions in Python 3 are actually faster than they were in Python 2! (And there is no longer a speed difference between the two.)
what: Thanks to general Python 3 speed work, both forms became faster than in Python 2 and the speed difference between them disappeared, removing the performance argument for the leak.

quote: in Python 3, we decided to fix the "dirty little secret" of list comprehensions by using the same implementation strategy as for generator expressions ... the 'x' in the list comprehension temporarily shadows but does not override the 'x' in the surrounding scope.
what: Python 3 fixed the leak by implementing list comprehensions with the same strategy as generator expressions, so the loop variable only shadows the outer one.

quote: we decided not to guess in this case, and the generator comprehension was required to have a single expression ... after its 'in' keyword. But at the time we didn't want to break existing code using the (already hugely popular) list comprehensions.
what: Faced with the ambiguity, they chose not to guess and required a single expression after the genexp's 'in', while not breaking existing list-comprehension code.

quote: Python 3 also supports set comprehensions and dictionary comprehensions. These are straightforward extensions of the list comprehension idea.
what: Python 3 also supports set and dict comprehensions as straightforward extensions of the list comprehension idea.

quote: The integer division operation (//) and its sibling, the modulo operation (%), go together and satisfy a nice mathematical relationship (all variables are integers)
what: Integer division (//) and modulo (%) are treated as a pair that must satisfy one mathematical relationship.

open: whether the floor rule should extend to floating point modulo is left unresolved.
quote: Tim Peters ... has expressed some worry about my desire to extend these rules to floating point modulo. He's probably right; the truncate-towards-negative-infinity rule can cause precision loss for x%1.0 when x is a very small negative number. But that's not enough for me to break integer modulo, and // is tightly coupled to that
what: Tim Peters worried about extending these rules to floating point modulo; Guido concedes the floor rule can cause precision loss for x%1.0 when x is a very small negative number, but keeps integer modulo (and //, tightly coupled to it) unchanged.

quote: if one of the operands is negative, the result is floored, i.e., rounded away from zero (towards negative infinity)
what: For positive operands the result is unsurprising; the flooring behavior shows up (rounding away from zero, towards negative infinity) only when an operand is negative.

quote: I am using // instead of / -- this is Python 3 syntax, and also allowed in Python 2 to emphasize that you know you are invoking integer division. The / operator in Python 2 is ambiguous, since it returns a different result for two integer operands than for an int and a float or two floats
what: // is used instead of / deliberately: it is Python 3 syntax, also allowed in Python 2 to make clear one is invoking integer division, whereas / in Python 2 is ambiguous because it returns different results for two integers than for mixed int/float operands.

quote: In mathematical number theory, mathematicians always prefer the latter choice (see e.g. Wikipedia). For Python, I made the same choice
what: The flooring choice follows what mathematicians in number theory always prefer, and Guido made the same choice for Python.

quote: explain why integer division in Python returns the floor of the result instead of truncating towards zero like C
what: Integer division in Python returns the floor of the result instead of truncating towards zero as C does.

quote: there are some interesting applications of the modulo operation where the sign of a is uninteresting
what: The reason given is that in some applications of modulo the sign of a is uninteresting; the POSIX-timestamp-to-time-of-day computation (t % 86400) works out with the floor rule even for times before 1970 expressed as negative numbers, where truncation would give a meaningless result.

quote: For negative b, by the way, everything just flips, and the invariant becomes:
what: For negative b everything flips and the invariant becomes 0 >= r > b.

quote: b*q + r = a and 0 <= r < b
what: The relationship chosen is b*q + r = a with 0 <= r < b, stated for non-negative a and b.

quote: if you truncate q towards zero, r will become negative, so that the invariant changes to 0 <= abs(r) < otherwise, you can floor q towards negative infinity, and the invariant remains 0 <= r < b
what: Extending the relation to negative a (with b positive) forces a choice: truncating q towards zero makes r negative and changes the invariant, or flooring q towards negative infinity keeps the invariant 0 <= r < b.

quote: Probably the hardware didn't do this at the time C was designed. And the hardware probably didn't do it this way because in the oldest hardware, negative numbers were represented as \"sign + magnitude\" rather than the two's complement representation
what: C probably truncates because the hardware did so when C was designed, which in turn stems from old hardware representing negatives as sign+magnitude or one's complement rather than two's complement.

open: qualified with "As far as I am aware".
quote: As far as I am aware, B was the first actually     published (and implemented) language to use indentation for     grouping.
what: Meertens claims B was, as far as he is aware, the first published and implemented language to use indentation for grouping, noting occam (1983) and Miranda (1985) came later and so could not be the source.

quote: the latter delimiters were also dropped in      B2, leaving pure     indentation as the sole indicator of grouping.
what: Meertens reports that once indentation was mandatory the separate delimiters were redundant, so they were progressively dropped (no BEGIN in B1, END IF/END FOR dropped in B2), leaving pure indentation as the sole indicator of grouping.

quote: Karin Dewar provided the inspiration for the use  of the colon in ABC (and hence in Python) leading up to the indentation, not for indentation itself.
what: Guido corrects an earlier account: the Dewar story is the origin of the colon in ABC (and hence Python), not of the indentation. He reports this from Lambert Meertens' email.

quote: here the scientists realized that the misunderstanding would have been avoided if there had been a colon at the end of that line.
what: Meertens recounts the Jabłonna design session where Robert Dewar's wife, reading a syntax, asked whether 'FOR i ...' applied to the following lines and not just that line; the scientists realized a colon at the end of the line would have avoided the misunderstanding, which is how the colon was conceived.

quote: the desire to have     the program text look neat and be suggestive of the meaning,     codifying what was already common practice but not enforced.
what: Meertens states the origin of indentation in ABC was the desire for the program text to look neat and suggest its meaning, codifying a practice that was already common but not enforced.

quote: The indentation was supposed to be added, like pretty printing, by a     dedicated B editor, and the user had no control over this
what: Meertens reports that B0, the first design in the sequence leading to ABC, had non-optional indentation for grouping, added by a dedicated editor, with the user unable to turn it off or modify it; it was supplemented by BEGIN/END delimiters.

open: stated as a possible influence ("may have been"), not settled.
quote: The     decision to remove the noise of BEGIN ... END     may have been influenced by [PL75], which actually advocated using     pure indentation for grouping.
what: Meertens notes the decision to remove the BEGIN...END "noise" may have been influenced by Plauger's [PL75], which advocated pure indentation for grouping.

quote: the invariant that when two / slices are adjacent, the first slice's end index is the second slice's / start index is just too beautiful to ignore.
what: The decisive beauty is the invariant that for adjacent slices the first slice's end index equals the second slice's start index, illustrated by splitting a string at i and j into a[:i], a[i:j], a[j:].

quote: It would be nice if both of these could be / expressed as without awkward +1 or -1 compensations.
what: A criterion for a good notation is that these use cases be expressible without awkward +1 or -1 corrections.

quote: Using closed intervals, you'd have to / write a[i:i+n-1] for the n items starting at i.
what: Under 1-based indexing with closed intervals, the n items starting at i require the awkward a[i:i+n-1].

quote: most common use cases for slicing are \"get the first n items\" and \"get / the next n items starting at i\"
what: He frames the decision around the two most common slicing use cases: getting the first n items and getting the next n items starting at i, the former being a special case of the latter.

open: He does not reconstruct the full comparison for other use cases.
quote: TBH / this is where my memory gets fuzzy, but I think I was swayed by the / elegance of half-open intervals.
what: When pushing the index:length convention against other use cases his memory is uncertain, but he believes the elegance of half-open intervals swayed him.

open: He raises index:length as a possible improvement but does not resolve how it works for other use cases.
quote: So perhaps using the / slice length would be more elegant with 1-based indexing? ... And this is in fact what ABC did -- it used a different / notation so you could write a@i|n.
what: An alternative he considered is a start-and-length (index:length) slice convention, which might suit 1-based indexing; ABC in fact did this with its own notation a@i|n.

quote: Using half-open intervals just isn't very elegant when / combined with 1-based indexing.
what: With 1-based indexing, half-open intervals are not elegant; getting the first n elements forces either closed intervals or a start-and-length slice notation.

quote: ABC, one of Python's predecessors, / used 1-based indexing, while C, the other big influence, used 0-based.
what: Python's two main predecessors pulled in opposite directions on indexing: ABC used 1-based, C used 0-based; his earlier languages (Algol, Fortran, Pascal) used 1-based or variable-based.

quote: I think that one of the issues that helped me decide / was slice notation.
what: Van Rossum attributes his choice of Python's indexing base largely to how slice notation would work out; slicing was the deciding issue.

quote: Using / 0-based indexing, half-open intervals, and suitable defaults (as Python / ended up having), they are beautiful: a[:n] and a[i:i+n]
what: The combination Python adopted, 0-based indexing with half-open intervals and suitable defaults, makes those use cases come out cleanly as a[:n] and a[i:i+n].

quote: The type of a type was always a\nspecial type object, which you could call a meta-type, to be recognized\nbecause it was its own type.
what: The type of a type was always a special type object, a meta-type, recognized because it is its own type.

quote: whether Python's metaclass design came from Ruby. It did not.
what: Python's metaclass design did not come from Ruby; the author corrects a speculation to the contrary.

quote: New-style classes were just the second or third iteration of the idea.
what: New-style classes were the second or third iteration of the metaclass idea in Python, which the author had written about in 1998.

quote: I was inspired to implement new-style classes by a very\nspecific book, \"Putting Metaclasses to Work\" by Ira Forman and Scott\nDanforth
what: The author was inspired to implement new-style classes by the book "Putting Metaclasses to Work" by Ira Forman and Scott Danforth.

quote: Ruby was in fact\ninspired by Python. Mats once told me that his inspiration was 20%\nPython, 80% Perl, and that Larry Wall is his hero.
what: The author reports that Ruby was inspired by Python, citing what Matz told him: 20% Python, 80% Perl, with Larry Wall as his hero. (reported by Matz)

quote: Smalltalk's bytecode was a bigger influence of Python's\nbytecode though.
what: Smalltalk's bytecode was a bigger influence on Python's bytecode, which the author had read about in a book by Adele Goldberg and others.

quote: I was only vaguely aware of Smalltalk at the time; I\nremember being surprised by its use of metaclasses (which is quite different from that in Python or Ruby!) when I read about\nthem much later.
what: The author was only vaguely aware of Smalltalk at the time and found its use of metaclasses, which differs from Python's or Ruby's, surprising when he read about it much later.

quote:
even Python's original design (in 1990, published in
1991) had the notion that 'type' was itself an object. The type pointer
in any object has always been a pointer to a special object, whose
"data" was a bunch of C function pointers implementing the behavior of
other objects, similar to a C++ vtable.
what: Even Python's original 1990 design held that 'type' was itself an object; every object's type pointer points to a special object whose data is C function pointers implementing behavior, like a C++ vtable.

quote: In Python 2.6, we added a built-in function named 'bytes'... Should your code now be considered invalid? There's no reason for that, and in fact your code will be fine.
what: Adding a new built-in (e.g. `bytes` in 2.6) must not invalidate existing code that used that name as a variable; such code stays valid.

quote: The answer is subtle, and has to do with consistency and evolution of the language.
what: Assignment to built-in names is allowed by design, for reasons of consistency and the evolution of the language; nobody can list all built-ins, and forbidding their use as names would surprise programmers.

quote: the left-hand side of the assignment operator (=) must be a variable, and a literal is not a variable. (The exact definition of variable is complex, since some things that look like expressions are also considered to be variables, such as d[k], (a, b), and foo.bar -- but not f() or () or 42.
what: The left-hand side of an assignment must be a variable; a literal is not one. The definition of variable is complex, covering d[k], (a, b), foo.bar but not f(), () or 42, and is shared with the del statement.

quote: The parser had no special knowledge of None -- just like it doesn't have special knowledge of built-in types like int, float or str... All of these are treated by the parser as identifiers, and when your code is being interpreted they are looked up just like any other names
what: Originally None, like built-in types and exceptions, was just a built-in name; the parser gives these no special knowledge and treats them as identifiers looked up at interpretation time, producing the same parse tree as any name.

quote: if you really want to mess with your readers, you can write code that reassigns built-ins
what: Because built-ins are ordinary names, code can reassign them (e.g. `int = float`), which lets one write confusing code.

quote: the all-caps form of the name suggests to the reader that it is probably not changed anywhere in the code... but this is just a convention, and the Python parser doesn't know about that convention, nor does it enforce it.
what: A constant is distinct from a literal: an all-caps identifier like MAX_LEVELS is a convention the parser neither knows nor enforces, while 15 is a literal.

quote: The important thing to remember about keywords is that a keyword cannot be used to name a variable (or function, class, etc.).
what: The defining property of a keyword is that it cannot be used to name a variable, function, class, etc.

quote: A keyword, in the context of defining the syntax of a language, also known as a reserved word, is something that looks like an identifier in the language, but from the parser's point of view act like a token of the language.
what: A keyword (reserved word) looks like an identifier but the parser treats it as a token of the language; an identifier is letters, digits and underscores not starting with a digit.

quote: A literal, on the other hand, is an element of an expression that describes a constant value... Literals are recognized by the parser, and the exact rules for how literals are parsed are often quite subtle.
what: A literal is an element of an expression that describes a constant value, recognized by the parser, with subtle parsing rules.

quote: the parser treats numeric and string literals as different from identifiers... the first three will still be accepted by the parser (<name> = <name>), while the swapped version of the second set will be rejected (<literal> = <name> is invalid).
what: Numeric and string literals produce a different parse tree from names, so `<name> = <name>` is accepted either way round while `<literal> = <name>` is rejected.

quote: at least we don't have to worry about breaking working code by merely adding something to the language. The (small) price we pay for this is the possibility that some joker intentionally redefines a built-in
what: Unlike keywords, new built-ins don't break working code, so adding them is cheap; the only price is a joker redefining one, which Guido judges minor among the many ways to write unreadable code.

quote: many proposed new features have been killed because they would require a new keyword; others have been modified to avoid that need.
what: Many proposed features were killed or modified because they would need a new keyword; adding one triggers a deprecation campaign a release ahead, with `from __future__ import` as an opt-in.

quote: None is a singleton object (meaning there is only one None), used in many places in the language and library to represent the absence of some other value.
what: None is a singleton object used throughout the language and library to represent the absence of some other value.

quote: In the end we decided that there was no downside to making None a keyword (there is no code that actually assigns to it) and it might make some code a tiny bit faster, or catch rare typos.
what: Making None a keyword was decided because there was no downside (no code assigns to it) and it might speed up code a little or catch rare typos; the one-time cost to parser and docs was small.

open: Whether the performance concern (two dictionary lookups making None slow) was actually founded is left uncertain.
quote: Why did we eventually make None a reserved word? Frankly, the reasons were perhaps mostly social... None is so central to using Python that you really can't be using Python without knowing about None.
what: None was eventually made a reserved word for mostly social reasons: it is so central that users were horrified assignment to it was allowed; a secondary concern was that evaluating None was slow, needing two dictionary lookups.

open: Whether constructs like `{'foo': 42}` are literals is left unsettled; Guido would prefer another name, noting the reference calls these "displays".
quote: My answer is that they are both. They are keywords because that's how the parser recognizes them. They are literals because that's their role in expressions and because they stand for constant values.
what: None/True/False are both keywords (how the parser recognizes them) and literals (their role in expressions, standing for constant values).

quote: everyone using Python has to know about all the reserved words in the language... For this reason, we try to keep the list of reserved words small, and the core developers hem and haw a lot before adding a new reserved word
what: Every reserved word must be known by everyone using Python, since it can never be used as a name anywhere; therefore the list is kept small and new keywords are added reluctantly.

quote: by the time Python 3 came around, when we looked at opportunities for cleaning up the language, we found that it was logical to make True and False keywords, by analogy to None.
what: Once defining one's own True/False became frowned upon, Python 3's cleanup made True and False keywords by analogy to None.

quote: we definitely did not want to break any packages that were defining their own True and False constants... essentially our hand was forced in this case, and we had to introduce True and False as built-in constants, not as keywords.
what: True and False had to be introduced as built-in constants rather than keywords because people had defined their own True/False constants, and backward compatibility (including running on earlier Python versions) forced that choice.

quote: Added new builtin function bool() and new builtin constants True and ... False to ease backporting of code developed for Python 2.3.
what: bool, True and False were also added in Python 2.2.1, which was a bugfix release, to ease backporting of code developed for Python 2.3.

quote: in 2.3, bool is a new type; in 2.2.1, bool() is a built-in function and the constants are just ints.
what: The bool in 2.2.1 differed from 2.3: in 2.3 bool is a new type, while in 2.2.1 bool() is a built-in function and True/False are just ints equal to 1 and 0.

quote: It was formally introduced in Python 2.3, as a new type with two constants, and the type was introduced in PEP 285 ("Adding a bool type").
what: The bool type was formally introduced in Python 2.3 as a new type with two constants, through PEP 285.

quote: That's a breakneck pace compared to how we do things a decade later!
what: The compressed chronology of PEP 285's creation, acceptance and finalization against the release dates reflects a much faster pace of doing things than a decade later.

quote: This was the last (and the most criticized) time we added a new feature in a bugfix release -- we'd never do that these days.
what: Adding a new feature in a bugfix release was the most criticized such instance and would not be done now; expressed as a change in practice.

quote: Writing up the reasons why True and False, when introduced, weren't reserved words
what: When True and False were introduced, they were deliberately not made reserved words; Guido notes he was writing up the reasons for this choice.

quote: I was not familiar with more advanced techniques, or I deemed them too inefficient.
what: He did not use more advanced parsing techniques, being unfamiliar with them or judging them too inefficient, as he believes most parser workers did then.

quote: Converting EBNF to BNF and taking it from there would cause awkward extra parse tree node types, so I don't think that would have been an improvement.
what: Converting EBNF to BNF and working from there would cause awkward extra parse-tree node types, so he does not think that would have been an improvement.

quote: For the lexer I decided I would not use a generator ... the version of Lex that I was familiar with would just segfault when trying to scan a token longer than 255 bytes (really!). Also I figured that indentation would be hard to teach to a lexer generator.
what: He chose not to use a generator for the lexer: he thought less of Lex than of Yacc (the Lex he knew would segfault on tokens longer than 255 bytes), and figured indentation would be hard to teach a lexer generator.

open: Stated with "I think", as a recollection.
quote: the parsing engine ... still works with parsing tables derived from such rules through the regex -> NFA -> DFA transformation; I think the requirement not to have any empty productions was required here.
what: He believes the parsing engine still works with parsing tables derived from such rules through the regex -> NFA -> DFA transformation, with a requirement of no empty productions.

quote: The original was actually the first code I wrote for Python. Although technically I had to write the lexer first (pgen and Python share their lexer, pgen just doesn't have any uses for most tokens).
what: The original pgen was the first code written for Python, though the lexer had to come first because pgen and Python share a lexer.

quote: I decided to design something vaguely like Python, implemented in Python, and decided that I wanted to reuse pgen, but with a backend in Python, using tokenize.py as the lexer. So I just rewrote the exact algorithm from pgen in Python
what: pgen2 arose at a startup (Elemental Security) where, tasked to design a custom security-assertion language, he designed something vaguely like Python, implemented in Python, and rewrote pgen's exact algorithm in Python using tokenize.py as the lexer.

quote: it made sense to use those tools for 2to3. (It was easy to generate a Python parser with it because the input format was identical to the original pgen -- I just had to feed the Grammar file into the tool. :-)
what: Because pgen2's input format was identical to the original pgen, it was easy to generate a Python parser by feeding it the Grammar file, and the open-sourced tooling was later used for 2to3.

quote: It certainly did not change the power beyond LL(1), nor did it reduce the power. And yes by "regular expressions" I meant the EBNF conventions -- I'm not sure that at the time "EBNF" was a well-defined notation
what: The regex notation did not change the parsing power beyond LL(1), nor reduce it; by "regular expressions" he meant the EBNF conventions, noting EBNF may not have been a well-defined notation at the time.

quote: UPDATE March 2019: Python 3.8 will drop the C version of pgen, in favor of a tweaked version of pgen2.
what: Python 3.8 will drop the C version of pgen in favor of a tweaked version of pgen2.

quote: the reason I used regular expressions was probably to make the grammar easier to read ... no helper rules with awkward names, and [optional] parts or repeated* parts are closer to how I think about a typical language's syntax.
what: The reason he used regular expressions was probably to make the grammar easier to read: after resolving conflicts with rewrites the grammar was not easy to read, and regex avoided helper rules with awkward names, with [optional] and repeated* parts closer to how he thinks about a language's syntax.

quote: I had one improvement over that that I wanted to try out: using regular expressions (sort of) instead of the standard BNF format. The Dragon book had also taught me how to turn regular expressions into DFAs, so I combined all that and pgen was born.
what: Building on LL(1) parser-generation and the Dragon book's regex-to-DFA technique, he wanted to try one improvement: using regular expressions instead of the standard BNF format, and from combining these pgen was born.

open: He does not quite recall why he did it this way ("I don't quite recall why I did things this way", line 18).
quote: I may have seen this as a new (to me) way of addressing the various conflicts that may occur without adding helper rules. E.g. what that page calls left-factoring ... I would rewrite instead as A -> X [Y Z].
what: Looking back, he may have seen the regex approach as a new way of addressing grammar conflicts without adding helper rules, e.g. rewriting left-factoring (A -> X | X Y Z becoming A -> X B; B -> Y Z | empty) instead as A -> X [Y Z].

quote: There are actually two pgens. The original, in C, and a rewrite in Python, under lib2to3/pgen2.
what: There are two parser generators for Python, the original written in C and a later rewrite in Python living under lib2to3/pgen2, both written by the author.

open: This "has turned out to be a double-edged sword" (line 34), later requiring a parse-tree-to-AST step driven by a separate generator to simplify the byte code generator.
quote: the parse tree nodes produced by the parsing engine would have a variable number of children ... A simple check in the code generator would then be needed to determine which alternative the parser had encountered.
what: Another idea was that parse-tree nodes have a variable number of children (e.g. A -> X [Y Z] yields a node with 1 or 3 children), with a simple check in the code generator to tell which alternative was parsed.

quote: The reason for writing my own parser generator was that at the time the landscape of parser generators ... was pretty sparse ... I had used Yacc in college ... but for some reason I didn't like it much; IIRC I found it hard to reason about what the limitations on an LALR(1) grammar would be.
what: The author wrote his own parser generator because the available options were sparse (Yacc, or hand-written parsers) and he disliked Yacc, finding it hard to reason about the limits of an LALR(1) grammar.

quote: If I had to do it all over again I might opt for a more powerful parsing engine, perhaps a version of LALR(1) ... the rule 'arg: [NAME =] expr' is not a valid rule, since NAME occurs in the FIRST-set of expr and the algorithm doesn't handle that. IIRC LALR(1) can handle it. But keyword args were several years in the future ... and I didn't want to redo the parser at that point.
what: Doing it over, he might choose a more powerful parsing engine such as LALR(1)/Yacc/Bison, since several grammar areas need more power than LL(1), e.g. keyword args where 'arg: [NAME =] expr' is not valid because NAME is in the FIRST-set of expr; LALR(1) can handle it, but keyword args came years later and he did not want to redo the parser then.
